planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; the deep red center intensifies through cool weather and fades least where drainage and light are both strong.

directions: Red Heart forms compact green rosettes with a bold ruby-red center that expands to color nearly the whole rosette during the cool days of late winter and early spring, then recedes to a defined core through summer heat. Grow it in lean, gritty soil with sharp drainage in full sun to partial sun, setting offsets directly on the soil surface rather than burying the crown. In midsummer it sends up short stalks of star-shaped pink flowers with burgundy bracts, and like all sempervivums the flowering rosette is monocarpic and dies afterward while surrounding chicks continue the clump. It is fully hardy through winter, tolerating snow cover and freezing temperatures without protection, making it a reliable choice for rock gardens, troughs, and stone wall crevices.

planting.note: Plant offsets in average to poor, sandy or rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun; this vigorous German hybrid spreads readily by stolons and needs room to colonize.

directions: A German hybrid dating to the late 1970s, Bronco is prized for reliable, strong seasonal color change: rosettes shift between green with purple tips, warm red-and-yellow tones, and a deep overall purple in cold winter weather. It spreads unusually vigorously for a sempervivum, sending out numerous stoloniferous offsets that let a single plant fill in a dense carpet within a couple of seasons, making it a strong groundcover choice for rock gardens and dry slopes. Grow in poor to average, sandy or rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun, where its color and vigor are both best expressed. Its dependable performance and long season of color earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

planting.note: Set offsets on lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; strong direct light is needed to develop the deepest burgundy leaf color, especially in summer.

directions: Terracotta Baby is a small-statured cultivar whose narrow, curling leaves fold inward around a bright green center, framed by fleshy burgundy outer foliage that deepens to near-maroon in cold weather and brightens to fiery red-orange through summer heat. Its diminutive rosette size and tightly curled leaf form make it a distinctive choice for miniature succulent gardens, troughs, and fairy gardens where larger sempervivums would overwhelm the scale. Grow in lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun, since strong light is essential to both its color intensity and its compact, tidy habit. As with all hens and chicks, individual rosettes are monocarpic and are steadily replaced by offsets, keeping the clump going indefinitely.

planting.note: Plant container stock in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool growing season; branches root easily from stem cuttings.

directions: Garnet forms a dense, freely branching mound of glossy rosettes that are two-toned, with wine-red margins fading into a bright apple-green center that persists even in the heat of summer, earning it the nickname Irish Eyes. It grows considerably larger and bushier over time than many aeonium cultivars, eventually reaching several feet across as branches keep producing new rosettes. Golden, star-shaped flower clusters appear on mature rosettes in spring, after which those individual rosettes die back while the rest of the shrub continues growing. Grow in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, watering through the cool season and letting the plant rest through summer dormancy.

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in lean, fast-draining soil; the sharpest pink and cream variegation develops with strong light and cool temperatures.

directions: Mardi Gras is a patented variegated selection bred from a cross involving Aeonium 'Velour', with compact rosettes striped in lemon-yellow and emerald green that blush pink to burgundy at the leaf margins, especially under bright light and cool weather. Its coloring shifts distinctly with the seasons: winter rosettes are greener and fuller with rounded leaf tips, while summer rosettes turn redder and more compact with flatter tips. It offsets readily from the base of the main rosette, gradually forming a colorful cluster well suited to containers where its variegation can be appreciated up close. Grow in lean, gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun to bright light, watering during the cool growing season and reducing water in summer.
sources: Huntington Botanical Gardens International Succulent Introductions

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; branching stems allow easy propagation by stem cuttings allowed to callus before planting.

directions: Bred in 1976 by hybridizer Jack Catlin from a cross of Aeonium canariense and Aeonium arboreum 'Zwartkop', Velour bears upright branching stems topped with glossy, velvety-textured rosettes in dark chocolate-purple that catch light differently than the flatter black sheen of Zwartkop. Its parentage gives it a somewhat larger, softer rosette than typical black aeoniums, with a bright green heart visible at the rosette's center when young. It grows into a shrubby, multi-branched plant a few feet tall over time and produces golden racemes of star-shaped flowers in late spring, though not every plant blooms. Grow in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, watering regularly during the cool season since aeoniums have shallow roots and dry out faster than many other succulents.

planting.note: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; this cultivar tolerates both heat and light frost better than most aeoniums.

directions: Named for its hybridizer, the late Jack Catlin, this cultivar bears low clumps of glossy, brilliant burgundy-red rosettes six to eight inches wide, each with a bright apple-green heart at the center that contrasts sharply with the darker outer leaves. Unlike most aeoniums, its rosettes do not die after flowering, so the plant keeps building a fuller, more permanent clump year after year rather than needing constant offset replacement. It also shows unusually good tolerance for both summer heat and brief light frost compared with other dark-leaved aeonium hybrids, extending its usable range slightly beyond the typical zone 9b-11 aeonium territory. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade for the deepest color.
sources: Huntington Botanical Gardens International Succulent Introductions

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; this hybrid clumps steadily and divides easily once several offsets have formed.

directions: Old Man Silver is a long-cultivated Gasteria hybrid grown for its thick, tongue-shaped leaves densely covered in raised silvery-white warty tubercles that give the whole rosette a frosted, textured appearance distinct from the smoother-leaf species. It has also served as a notable parent in later Gasteria breeding, including the well-known 'Little Warty' hybrid, thanks to its strong warty-texture trait. Slow to moderate growing, it offsets steadily at the base to form a tidy clump that can be divided for propagation once new rosettes are well rooted. Grow in bright, indirect light or partial shade in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried completely, since it tolerates lower light far better than most succulents.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Flavida Pig's Ear (Finger Aloe, Grey Sticks)

planting.note: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; the powdery chalk-blue coating on the leaves is easily rubbed off, so handle transplants gently and avoid overhead watering.

directions: Originally collected in South Africa's Eastern Cape, this form of pig's ear differs from the broad, rounded-leaf species by its slender, finger-like leaves held on sprawling, decumbent branches, giving rise to the common names finger aloe and grey sticks. The foliage carries a powdery chalk-blue-gray coating and is often tipped in dull red, distinct from the flatter, more paddle-shaped leaves of the typical species and from the ruffled edges of Silver Waves. It spreads outward over time into a low, wide shrub, eventually reaching several feet across while staying under two feet tall. In spring, umbrella-like clusters of pale orange, bell-shaped flowers rise well above the foliage on tall stalks, and the plant roots readily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before planting in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun.
